blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The median is the middle value of a dataset arranged in order: as many observations lie below it as above it.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The mean is pulled by every value’s size, including extreme ones. The median depends only on position: which value sits in the middle once everything is sorted. One very large or very small value shifts the mean a lot but moves the middle position little or not at all.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Five children’s weights, sorted: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 kg. Median = 11 kg, the same as the mean because these data are symmetric.

Now one child is severely malnourished and weighs 2 kg instead of 9: sorted weights 2, 10, 11, 12, 13. The mean drops to 9.6 kg. The median stays at 11 kg, because the middle value did not move. For an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values: today’s 30 sorted weights have 11.6 and 11.8 kg in positions 15 and 16, so the raw median is 11.7 kg.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
With grouped data the individual values are gone, so you locate the median class (the class containing the (N/2)th observation) from the cumulative frequencies (recall §1.4.3) and assume its f values are spread evenly across its width h. Let L be the lower boundary of the median class and cf the cumulative frequency of all classes below it. You need N/2 − cf more observations after L. Each observation in the median class occupies h/f of the width, so walk (N/2 − cf) × h/f into the class:

Median = L + [(N/2 − cf) ÷ f] × h

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: grouped median
blocks.html:
Today’s 30 children: cumulative frequencies 5, 17, 26, 30.

  1. N/2 = 15. The 15th child lies in the class whose cumulative frequency first reaches 15: 10 to <12 (cumulative 17).
  2. L = 10, cf = 5 (the class below), f = 12, h = 2.
  3. Median = 10 + [(15 − 5) ÷ 12] × 2 = 10 + 1.667 = 11.67 kg.

The raw median was 11.7 kg. The small gap comes from the even-spread assumption.

points.html: Odd n: the middle value after sorting, position (n + 1)/2. Even n: the average of the two middle values.

Grouped data: Median = L + [(N/2 − cf) ÷ f] × h. Use the lower class boundary for L (for “10 to <12” this book uses 10, ignoring the 0.05-kg rounding shift noted in §1.4.2), and cf of the classes below the median class.
The median is robust: extreme values barely move it. This is its main practical advantage over the mean.
The median suits ordinal data and skewed quantitative data; the mean needs interval or ratio data and describes roughly symmetric distributions best (§2.5).
The median is the value that minimises the sum of absolute distances Σ|x − c|; the mean minimises the sum of squared distances. Both facts are derived in §3.5 and §3.6.
